stories.topic: Blood Viscosity, Sweat, and the Hack of Dehydration Training
stories.summary: The average human body has six litres of blood; lose one litre as sweat and the blood becomes meaningfully thicker (about 16.6% loss on the base), making it harder for the heart to pump. That is why we feel cardio-tired when dehydrated and why drinking water during exercise feels so restorative. Ajay's twist: under controlled treadmill conditions you could deliberately train slightly dehydrated to amp up cardiac load. Amit jokes that as a Bengali he is now relieved he can just stop drinking water and walk gently to get a workout.
stories.insight: A great example of using mechanism, not folk wisdom, to design training. Once you understand why dehydration makes cardio harder (viscosity, pump load), you can both prevent fatigue (drink) and intentionally use it as a stress (controlled, with safety net). The same lesson cuts the other way too: marathoners die from drinking too much water, so 'more water' is not a universal good.

stories.topic: The Pill Case That Lets You Be a Zombie One Day, a Planner the Other Six
stories.summary: Ajay's sub-rupees-300 pick of a tool he uses every day: a plastic pill case with seven daily compartments, each split into morning/afternoon/evening. He fills it once a week (taking on the cognitive burden in one concentrated act), and the rest of the week he just blindly obeys the box. The box also remembers for him: 'did I take the lunch dose?' is answered by glancing at whether the tablet is still there.
stories.insight: A clean illustration of offloading state from your head to the world. Concentrate all the thinking once a week, then drop into autopilot for six days. Memory and willpower are scarce; use external scaffolding so they don't have to be spent on routine.

stories.topic: Starbucks as a Forcing Function for Discipline
stories.summary: Amit built an awesome home office (sit-stand desk, all the tech) but still finds himself slipping into hours of online bullet chess. So he often hauls himself to a Starbucks, where simply being visible to other people sitting with laptops makes him feel sheepish about playing chess and forces him to actually work. He confesses this is an ongoing battle, not a solved problem.
stories.insight: Even people who appear hyper-productive struggle with discipline. The fix is environmental, not heroic: design a context where the cheap dopamine option carries a small social cost. The honest admission ('I struggle as much as you do') is itself the lesson.

stories.topic: Modafinil, Keto, and a 100-Point ELO Swing
stories.summary: Amit has sleep apnea (for which modafinil is prescribed) and uses it to focus during marathon recordings. He notes a striking observation: on days he is on modafinil or strictly keto, his Chess.com bullet rating climbs by ~100 ELO points; off them it drops back. Since he is not actively training to improve, the swing is purely cognitive state. He stresses the prescription/medical caveat but treats the rating as a candid biomarker for mental sharpness.
stories.insight: Use unrelated activities you already do as instruments. A daily ELO graph is, for him, a more honest measure of cognitive state than self-report. Anyone with a regular skill metric (chess rating, code review velocity, sketch output) has a free n-of-1 trial running.

stories.topic: Reading 100 Books Indiscriminately Beats 10 Carefully Curated Ones
stories.summary: Asked for a 'top ten bookshelf,' Amit refuses the premise. He argues that a primer-to-canon reading list is the wrong frame: in his experience, reading widely and indiscriminately, including a lot of fiction, builds a richer mental landscape than a small curated list. Get into the habit of picking up a book whenever you would otherwise pick up the phone.
stories.insight: Quantity creates the surface area on which serendipity can act. The 'right book at the right time' (as Ajay extends in his answer) is a matching problem; you can only match if you have a large catalogue in your head.

stories.topic: There Is No Objectively Great Book — Only the Right Book at the Right Time
stories.summary: Ajay extends Amit's reading argument with a stronger claim: he is no longer convinced any book is objectively great. Each of us is a trajectory through time ('no man can cross the same river twice'), and what matters is the matching process — the right book hitting at the right moment. He recalls explosive moments where a book from a trusted source (Lant Pritchett gave him both Seeing Like a State and The Functions of the Executive) landed at exactly the right time and rewired his thinking.
stories.insight: Two practical implications. (1) Lightly engage with a wide library so your mental index is dense — then matches can happen. (2) Hang out with people who know great books and respect their recommendations enough to actually read them; the trust is what gets the book past your filters into a serious read.

stories.topic: The CPAP Machine That Cured Acid Reflux, Not Sleep
stories.summary: Ajay (lightly sleep-apnoeic) started using a CPAP machine and got an unexpected second-order benefit. He had decades of acid reflux that left him waking with a sore throat or cold almost every morning. The pressurised air through the nasal mask kept stomach acid from rising at night — the morning sore throats vanished. The expected benefit (better sleep) was minor; the side effect was life-changing.
stories.insight: Interventions in complex systems produce side effects that often dwarf the intended effect. Stay alert to second-order changes whenever you start a new therapy, drug, or routine — the real value may be somewhere you weren't looking.

stories.topic: Ajay Hanging Off a Cliff and Saying 'Let's Solve This'
stories.summary: How Ajay broke his leg in January 2024: he fell off the edge of a hiking trail and was hanging by his hand from his friend Ayush, body covered in panic-sweat. Ayush — also stoic and rational — held him silently for about thirty seconds without a word. Then Ajay looked up and said, 'Let's solve this.' That was the entire conversation in the crisis.
stories.insight: A perfect distillation of Ajay's stated crisis-management rule from earlier in the episode: the bigger the crisis, the calmer you must become to summon your mind. The story shows the rule executed under extreme stress, between two people who didn't need to coordinate verbally because both had internalised the same heuristic.

recommendations.creator: Ingmar Bergman
recommendations.context: Bergman's 1957 masterpiece about an aging professor reflecting on his life — fittingly raised during a discussion of why aging societies make better cinema.
recommendations.reason: Amit's recommended best gateway into Bergman, who can otherwise feel inaccessible. A magnificent film about old age and growing old gracefully.

recommendations.item: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column arguing against the Malthusian framing of India's population.
recommendations.reason: Crystallises the 'people are brains, not stomachs' idea. Migration toward density (cities) is the dominant human story; treating people as stomachs is a condescending category error. Every supposed population problem is really a governance failure.

recommendations.item: Eamonn Butler's Primers (on Public Choice, Classical Liberalism, Hayek, Friedman)
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Compact primers on the foundational thinkers and ideas of classical liberalism.
recommendations.reason: When asked for an entry point to classical liberalism, Butler's primers are Amit's most reliable starting recommendation: short, lucid, and faithful to the source thinkers.

recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's classic on how state legibility and high-modernist planning produce disasters when they steamroll local knowledge.
recommendations.reason: Repeatedly cited by both hosts. Ajay credits Lant Pritchett for putting it in his hands at the right time; the book reshaped how he thinks about state-society interaction.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Orwell's collected essays — beyond the famous novels.
recommendations.reason: Amit's standing recommendation as a model of clear, morally serious prose; an education in both writing and thinking.

recommendations.creator: Chester Barnard
recommendations.context: A 1938 management classic on what executives actually do and how organisations behave.
recommendations.reason: Pointed to Ajay by Lant Pritchett. A profound batch of knowledge that opened up his thinking on organisational behaviour, applicable to firms and government bodies alike.

recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's account of early agrarian states and the costs of grain civilisations.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it one of the most perfect executions of a book he has read — if you want to learn the craft of writing a non-fiction book, study this. It reset his standards for the level of perfection a book can attain.

recommendations.creator: Alain Bertaud
recommendations.context: Bertaud's book on cities, urban planning, and how markets and rules shape urban form.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a masterpiece for anyone who wants to learn about cities and urban planning.

recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: Carlin's epic-scale narrative history podcast.
recommendations.reason: Amit's top podcast pick — quite amazing in the immersive, long-form way it tells history.

recommendations.creator: Sam Harris
recommendations.context: Sam Harris's interview podcast on philosophy, science, and current events.
recommendations.reason: Amit recommends it specifically as a study of the art of conversation — its flow and rhythm shaped his sense of how interviews can be conducted.

recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Rajagopalan's interview podcast on India.
recommendations.reason: Amit's favourite Indian podcast — Shruti does an incredible job of bringing diverse perspectives and rigorous analysis on India.

recommendations.creator: Milan Vaishnav
recommendations.context: Vaishnav's podcast on Indian politics, especially active around elections.
recommendations.reason: Amit's recommendation for understanding contemporary Indian politics from a fine thinker.

recommendations.creator: Milan Vaishnav
recommendations.context: Vaishnav's book on the nexus between crime and electoral politics in India.
recommendations.reason: A must-read on the role of criminal candidates in Indian politics.

recommendations.creator: Russ Roberts
recommendations.context: Roberts's long-running economics conversation podcast.
recommendations.reason: Long-running favourite of Amit's — Russ Roberts has also appeared on The Seen and the Unseen for an episode on conversation itself.

recommendations.creator: Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: Joseph's book on the genetic and historical origins of modern Indians.
recommendations.reason: Source of the powerful idea that India is not one population but thousands of small populations — the hidden cost of two thousand years of caste endogamy. Reshaped Amit's understanding of Indian history.

recommendations.item: Who We Are and How We Got Here
recommendations.creator: David Reich
recommendations.context: Reich's genetic-history account of human populations.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line 'India is not a large population, it is a collection of thousands of small populations,' which Amit uses to explain the genetic and economic costs of caste endogamy.

recommendations.item: Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Sowell's data-driven cross-country study of affirmative action policies.
recommendations.reason: Cited as the rigorous test of whether affirmative-action policies actually help the people they were designed to help. Amit invokes it as the empirical counter to lazy assumptions on either side.

recommendations.creator: Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Mohan's book on the linguistic history of the Indian subcontinent.
recommendations.reason: Amit's pointer for anyone curious about how Indian languages evolved and continue to mix and flatten.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column arguing that, in a competitive marketplace, profit is the highest form of philanthropy.
recommendations.reason: Crystallises Amit's reply to Milton Friedman's 'responsibility of business is to maximise profit': the only way to profit voluntarily is to make someone else better off (the double-thank-you moment). Nehru's dismissal of profit as a dirty word was, in his view, simply wrong.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's essay on how the form of a podcast (length, structure) shapes its content and the listener.
recommendations.reason: His written reflection on how moving from short interviews to four-, six-, eight-hour deep dives changed both the show and him. A five-hour conversation is not five times a one-hour conversation — it is a different beast.

recommendations.creator: Bjorn Lomborg
recommendations.context: Lomborg's data-driven examination of environmental claims, written more than 20 years ago.
recommendations.reason: Amit's takeaway from Lomborg's tracing of London and other Western cities: countries get heavily polluted on the way up and clean up as they grow rich. Growth and sustainability go together; the markets-vs-environment dichotomy is false.

recommendations.creator: Luke Burgis
recommendations.context: Burgis's accessible book on Rene Girard's theory of mimetic desire.
recommendations.reason: Amit's recommended primer on mimetic desire — the idea that we want what others want. Especially relevant when thinking about life-shaping decisions like marriage and children, which are often pure mimesis.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy, now in a paperback second edition with expanded reading-list end notes.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pick when asked how to learn India: the second edition pairs each of its 45 chapters with a curated reading list, making it a launching pad for systematic study of Indian economic policy.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman on the Minimum Wage
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Friedman's classic short-form argument that minimum wages price the lowest-skilled workers out of the market entirely.
recommendations.reason: Amit links this to clarify a basic economic point: a 15,000-rupee minimum wage doesn't lift workers worth less than that — it puts them out of work at zero. The poorest are hurt most by the law that claims to protect them.

recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta, Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Co-authored paper on how Indian businesses systematically misinvoice imports and exports to bypass exchange controls.
recommendations.reason: Quantifies the de-facto convertibility Indian businesses achieved despite formal capital controls — and supports Ajay's larger claim that cryptocurrencies are simply one more tool in the same long tradition.

recommendations.item: Praise for Intelligence Can Undermine Children's Motivation and Performance
recommendations.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
recommendations.context: Mueller and Dweck's classic experiment on praising children for intelligence vs. effort.
recommendations.reason: The empirical backbone of Amit's parenting advice: kids praised for being intelligent tried less hard and were more willing to cheat in subsequent tests; kids praised for effort kept trying. Praise effort, not attributes.

recommendations.creator: Jacob Bronowski
recommendations.context: Bronowski's series and book celebrating the trajectory of human knowledge across cultures.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's frame for refusing ethnic-greatness anxiety: the glory is the human journey, not lines on a map. He'd just rename it 'The Ascent of Humans.'

recommendations.creator: Indian Colours
recommendations.context: An online source of printed shirts.
recommendations.reason: One of the brands Ajay names when listeners ask about his now-iconic on-camera shirts.

core_ideas.explanation: A recurring frame: the Malthusian view of population sees humans as mouths that consume; the correct view sees them as minds that produce ideas, skills, and value. Migration flows are always toward density, not away — people vote with their feet for cities precisely because density creates prosperity. Every supposed 'too many people' problem is really a governance failure. And, as Amit notes, every person who calls population a problem somehow excludes themselves from the population.
core_ideas.quote: There is no such thing as too many people. People are brains, not stomachs.

core_ideas.concept: Universal Suffrage as a Civilisational Achievement
core_ideas.explanation: When asked whether voting should be restricted to those who pass a test, Amit refuses outright. The moment you create a bar, somebody decides what the bar is — and that somebody will exclude others. Education is not a guarantee of good ideas. India should be proud that it began with universal suffrage, including women voting before many advanced nations did. There is much wrong with the Indian republic, but this we got right.
core_ideas.quote: I think India should be proud that when we began, we began with universal suffrage.

core_ideas.concept: Caste Endogamy and the Thousands of Small Populations
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Tony Joseph and David Reich: roughly 2,000 years ago, an ideological strand from the Gangetic Belt enforced caste endogamy on what had been a millennium of intermingling migrants. The result is that India is genetically not one population but thousands of small ones. The cost is not only social but economic (small networks, low mobility) and medical (unique genetic-disease clusters). The real solvent, Amit argues, is economic growth — large urban networks where the cost of discrimination becomes high enough that markets erode it.
core_ideas.quote: If you're looking for a large population, look at the Han Chinese. India is really a collection of thousands of small populations. — David Reich

core_ideas.explanation: Lant Pritchett's distinction (used by Amit to diagnose intellectual dishonesty in development economics). National development asks the messy, hard, morally urgent questions: how do we end poverty? Kinky development tackles small, narrow questions with clean answers, gets you papers and tenure, and never makes a dent on the big problem. RCTs are the canonical example. The career incentives reward the kinky over the national.
core_ideas.quote: The moral imperative is to end poverty. The career imperative is to publish clean small studies.

core_ideas.concept: Spontaneous Order Is Descriptive, Not Normative
core_ideas.explanation: When pushed that patriarchy, caste, and global warming are also products of spontaneous order, Amit and Ajay agree but draw the right inference. Spontaneous order describes how systems emerge bottom-up — including bad ones. The fix for bad spontaneous orders is also bottom-up: societal change, market pressure, evolving values. Top-down impositions tend to fail and tend to be dangerous because the values of those at the top are unknown. The exception is genuine market failure (e.g. carbon emissions) where state intervention has a defined toolkit role.
core_ideas.quote: Whatever is imposed from the top of the top of the top, partly it doesn't work too well and partly it is truly dangerous because who knows what the values and the culture of the people at the top are.

core_ideas.concept: The Right Book at the Right Time (Matching, Not Canon)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's claim against canon-thinking: there is no objectively great book, because each of us is a different trajectory through time and books are explosive only when they meet us at the right moment. The job is therefore not to consume a curated top-ten list but to maintain a dense, light-engaged catalogue in your head and a community of trusted recommenders. The book that hit Ajay was Seeing Like a State — given by Lant Pritchett, taken seriously because Lant gave it, arriving when Ajay had been deep in the Indian state.
core_ideas.quote: What we need is a matching process where the right book shows up at the right time.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's strongest parenting advice, grounded in Mueller and Dweck's experiment. Children praised for intelligence ('you're so smart') tried less hard on subsequent tasks, slipped, and were more willing to cheat — they had been told they had a fixed asset to protect. Children praised for effort ('you tried so hard, you kept at it') just kept trying. The lesson generalises beyond children: any praise of fixed attributes makes the recipient defensive of an identity rather than willing to fail and learn.
core_ideas.quote: I simply wish that I had never thought I was intelligent and I had only assumed that I must try, try, try, harder and harder and harder.

core_ideas.concept: Profit = Philanthropy in a Competitive Marketplace
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's full reply to Milton Friedman's 'maximise profit' dictum. In a competitive marketplace with no market failures, the only way to profit voluntarily is to make someone else better off — every transaction is a 'double thank you' moment. Profit is therefore the highest form of philanthropy, scaled. Nehru's 'do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word' (to J.R.D. Tata) was simply wrong. The standard caveats: collusion with the state, market failures, and harm to others all break the equivalence.
core_ideas.quote: Profit is not a dirty word in a competitive marketplace. It is the highest form of philanthropy.

core_ideas.concept: Organizations vs. Institutions (and the Indian Confusion)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay insists the word 'institution' is too easily abused in Indian discourse. An institution is an aspiration, not a reality: an impersonal capability where people come and go but behaviour stays predictable and consistent. India, a backward state, is full of organisations that are personalised — their behaviour swings with whoever is in charge. The right toolkit for organisations is sceptical public-choice theory: people respond to incentives, are lazy, corrupt, power-seeking. Calling such an organisation an 'institution' grants it a virtue it has not earned.
core_ideas.quote: An institution is an impersonal capability where people come and people go, but the institution works in a predictable and consistent way.

core_ideas.concept: Power Adds Magnitude to the Vector You Already Are
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's revised view of technology after decades of optimism. He used to believe Moore's Law and the Internet would make the world better simply by giving people access to knowledge. Now he sees them as power amplifiers — they add magnitude to whoever you already are. If your character vector points toward good, technology amplifies the good; if it points the other way, technology amplifies the bad. The corollary, voiced by Amit: 'if power corrupts then we are all inherently corrupt.'
core_ideas.quote: When you achieve power you become more of what you really are.

core_ideas.explanation: A phrase Amit borrows from Sugata Srinivasaraju. He confesses what he calls his own life-mistake: being cosmopolitan but not rooted enough. The advice: build communities of choice (not just of circumstance), be globalised in your outlook, but stay rooted in the cultures you came from. Not everything in inherited culture is toxic; there is value worth carrying forward.
core_ideas.quote: I am cosmopolitan but I am not rooted enough. That is a lament I have.

core_ideas.concept: Three Behaviours to Denormalise: Noise, Celebrity Culture, and Contempt for Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's catalogue when asked what behaviours the modern world should denormalise. (1) Noise pollution — motorcycles, construction, marriage parties audible from a kilometre away, the casual infliction of sound on others. Pro tip: never rent near a temple or mosque. (2) Celebrity culture — we have built a world that reveres people famous only for being famous; the bubble persists because we keep inflating it. (3) Contempt for knowledge and expertise — the modern populist stance, where 'the person without the knowledge armed with the WhatsApp is cocky and says I look down on those who have knowledge.' Fifty years ago people lacked knowledge but respected it; today they lack it and despise it.
core_ideas.quote: Today the person without the knowledge armed with the WhatsApp is cocky and says I look down on the people who have knowledge.

core_ideas.concept: Judge Virtue by Action, Not Words
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's addendum to the denormalise list. Social media is an industrial-scale virtue-signalling machine; the loudest public moralists are often the most empty in their actual lives. Older feminists (Amit cites his episodes with women who worked in the field for 20-30 years) bemoan younger Twitter sloganeers who gain status within their tribes for words while doing no real work. Before being held up as virtuous, a person should have actually done something. 'Those who project the most virtue possess the least.'
core_ideas.quote: Those who project the most virtue possess the least.

core_ideas.concept: Communities of Choice, Not of Circumstance
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's frame for how to build life: the great fortune of being born into the modern era is that you can break away from the community of circumstance (caste, geography, family) and assemble a community of choice based on shared values and interests. The places you go and the things you have don't matter; what matters is the people you collect. Begin by collecting good people.

Ajay's stated rule, illustrated by Amit's cliffhanger story: the bigger the crisis, the more calm and collected you have to be — because that is the only state in which you can summon your mind to solve it. Panic is a luxury affordable only when stakes are low. Hanging from a friend's hand off a mountain edge, the right opening line is not a scream but 'let's solve this.'

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: On Bengali genius for hydration physics: Amit, hearing about blood viscosity and cardiac load — 'The Bengali in me is freaking delighted because I'm just thinking that I don't need to go running anymore. I can just stay away from water and walk around gently and the heart is still working.'
Ajay on AMA discipline: 'This shall be a low digressions episode, Amit. Done. We have too many questions. We have to respect them.'

Ajay's theory of cinema and median age: 'There's a thought that the quality of movies in a country is basically proportional to the median age. So when India was a very young country, the quality of the movies was atrocious. And as the country ages, we start getting better movies.'
Amit on infrastructure speed: Ajay says infrastructure takes long in 'any civilised country.' Amit interjects: 'Or fast, some might say. An uncivilised country.'

Amit on the writing course as ethical labour: 'You can't be too cynical and think of it only as revenue. In whatever you do, whether you're doing it for reach or revenue, you have to put your heart and soul.'
Amit on his pill regimen for the future listener: 'Ideally, dear reader, we want you to be so healthy that you never need pills at all — and for this it's also important that you hydrate properly.'

Ajay on the genie boon to fix India: he wants to take a time machine with a bag of books to Nehru, Gandhi, and Rajagopalachari. Amit pushes back — Ajay was receptive to Seeing Like a State only because he had been in the belly of the beast — but lets the wish stand.

On algorithmic beauty bringing tears: Ajay offers Amit a 'training' that would make him a master of computer programming so he can weep at perfect algorithms. Amit replies: 'Tears are coming to my eyes thinking of the amount of brute coercion that would be required to make me a master of computer programming.'

Mid-AMA interruption from real life: Ajay narrating a parent advice on praise-effort-not-intelligence breaks off mid-sentence with 'Aloo pyaaj is being sold down — do you want some aloo pyaaj? Aloo has a lot of carbs, pyaaj not so much.' The street vendor and the keto diet meet inside one sentence.
Mistakenly calling someone 'No One': asked by a viewer who calls themself 'No One,' Ajay deadpans 'No One says, Amit, what are your favourite podcasts.'
On rental tip-of-the-day: 'Look for any religious structure and keep far away from it. Like never rent a house that is close to a temple or a mosque because they'll just make so much noise.'
Bob Dylan: 'If you're not busy being born, you're busy dying' — Amit's anchor for why a specialist who refuses to engage with the wider world is busy dying.
Annie Dillard: 'How you spend your days, of course, is how you spend your life' — Amit's framing for what an aim in life should look like, day by day.
Richard Bach: 'What a caterpillar calls the end of the world, the master calls a butterfly' — Amit's quote in praise of apprenticing with a good master.
John Lennon: 'No time is wasted unless you feel it is wasted' — Amit's defence against the productivity-treadmill attitude to time.
John Stuart Mill's harm principle, invoked by Amit on company ethics: as long as a company is not infringing on someone's rights, the moral question of profit doesn't even arise.

Steve Jobs's advice to Jonathan Ive in the 1990s, recalled by Amit: 'Learn to say no to things that you love.' It is easy to say no to what you don't want; the discipline is saying no to all but one of the many things you do want.
Metcalfe's Law (network value scales as n^2), invoked by Ajay to explain why the Indian English-speaking network keeps gaining power as more nodes get connected.
Rene Girard's mimetic desire, via Luke Burgis: Amit's frame for why people get married and have children mostly because others do, without ever interrogating the trade-offs.

Jacob Bronowski's The Ascent of Man — the title from which Ajay borrows when he says he loves Ramanujan as much as Einstein, Gandhi as much as Nehru: 'I see the glory of the human journey... the ascent of man,' which Amit gently retitles The Ascent of Humans.
